pages.name: One arrow, two grids
pages.text: Your square grid is built from i, one step across, and j, one step up. The arrow to `(3, 3)` means 3 lots of i and 3 of j. Suppose Jennifer measures with her own two arrows, `b₁ = (2, 1)` and `b₂ = (−1, 1)`, written in your numbers. They make her slanted grid. Two lots of b₁ reach `(4, 2)`. One b₂ on the end reaches `(3, 3)`. So to her, the same arrow is `(2, 1)`. Her numbers mean nothing until you know her arrows.

pages.name: Her numbers to yours
pages.task: Her numbers are `(1, 2)`. Where does the arrow end on your grid?
pages.why: Her numbers are amounts. One lot of b₁ is `(2, 1)`. Two lots of b₂ are `(−2, 2)`. Nose to tail they reach `(0, 3)`.

pages.name: The matrix P
pages.text: To turn her numbers into yours, take 2 lots of b₁ and add 1 of b₂. You land on `(3, 3)`. A matrix times a column is exactly that sum. It is a mix of the matrix's columns. So put her arrows in as columns. `P = [2 −1; 1 1]`, and P times `(2, 1)` is `(3, 3)`. This is the [[change-of-basis matrix]]. Its columns are her arrows written in your numbers.

pages.name: Build a P
pages.task: A grid is made of `(1, 2)` and `(1, −1)`. Which matrix takes its numbers to yours?
pages.why: P has the grid's arrows as its columns. The first column is `(1, 2)`, and the second is `(1, −1)`. So `P = [1 1; 2 −1]`. Then P times any numbers on that grid gives yours.

pages.name: The way back
pages.text: To go from your numbers to hers, undo P with its inverse. P's determinant is `2 × 1 − (−1) × 1 = 3`. That is also the area of one cell of her grid. The area is not 0, so P has an inverse. It is `P⁻¹ = [1 1; −1 2] ÷ 3`. P⁻¹ times `(3, 3)` is `(6, 3) ÷ 3 = (2, 1)`. Multiply back with P to check.

pages.name: A move in her numbers
pages.text: A quarter turn anticlockwise is `M = [0 −1; 1 0]` in your numbers. She wants one matrix that takes her numbers in and gives her numbers out. Follow her `(2, 1)` along the strip. P rewrites it as your `(3, 3)`. M turns that to `(−3, 3)`. P⁻¹ brings it back to her numbers, `(0, 3)`. Three lots of b₂ do reach `(−3, 3)`. The first step goes on the right. So the turn, in her numbers, is P⁻¹MP.

pages.name: A simpler move
pages.text: Take `M = [3 1; 0 2]` and a new grid, `b₁ = (1, 0)` and `b₂ = (−1, 1)`. In the new grid's numbers, b₁ is `(1, 0)`. M stretches it to 3b₁, `(3, 0)`. b₂ is `(0, 1)`, and M stretches it to 2b₂, `(0, 2)`. Those are the columns, so `P⁻¹MP = [3 0; 0 2]`. This [[change of basis]] turns the move into two plain stretches. Lesson 6 finds such grids. Three-phase work uses one too. The Clarke transform turns three phase quantities into two parts at right angles.

pages.answer: Most arrows get no numbers on that grid
pages.why: `(4, 2)` is twice `(2, 1)`. Both lie on one line, so every mix stays on it. The cell area is `2 × 2 − 1 × 4 = 0`, so P has no inverse. Most arrows, like `(3, 3)`, get no numbers at all.
